query: We aim to synthesize an equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy via ink-extrusion additive manufacturing using a precursor blend of metallic and hydride powders. The process relies on the sequential thermal decomposition of hydrides (TaH0.5, NbH, HfH2, TiH2, ZrH2) to drive alloying, where decomposition temperatures correlate with hydride formation enthalpies. To prevent the formation of alpha-HCP phases induced by dissolved oxygen (an alpha-stabilizer) which would otherwise degrade mechanical properties, the sintering atmosphere must be strictly controlled using an oxygen getter. The goal is to achieve a nearly fully dense microstructure where slow cooling results in a dual-phase (alpha-BCC + beta-BCC) structure, but a rapid quench from the homogenization temperature traps a metastable single-phase beta-BCC structure. Propose a hypothesis for the specific oxygen getter material and sintering regime that balances dehydrogenation kinetics with oxygen scavenging, predict the resulting phase constitution and grain size after rapid quenching, and design a falsification experiment using in-situ X-ray diffraction to verify the sequence of phase transformations and the absence of alpha-Ti during the critical decomposition window.

generation.hypothesis: Utilizing a dual-stage sintering regime with a reactive calcium hydride (CaH2) oxygen getter, which decomposes to CaO and releases hydrogen at temperatures overlapping with the TaH0.5 decomposition window, will simultaneously achieve complete dehydrogenation of the precursor blend and reduce the oxygen partial pressure below 10^-15 atm, thereby preventing alpha-phase nucleation and enabling the retention of a metastable single-phase beta-BCC structure upon rapid quenching.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr precursor powder blend containing metallic powders and hydrides (TaH0.5, NbH, HfH2, TiH2, ZrH2) with an initial oxygen content of approximately 500-1000 ppm, mixed with 5 wt% CaH2 getter powder.
generation.intervention: Ink-extrusion additive manufacturing followed by a two-step thermal treatment: (1) a slow ramp to 900°C at 2°C/min in an inert argon atmosphere containing the CaH2 getter to facilitate sequential hydride decomposition and oxygen scavenging, followed by (2) rapid heating to 1250°C (homogenization) and immediate water quenching.
generation.conditions: Atmosphere: High-purity Argon (99.999%) with CaH2 getter present; Temperature profile: 900°C hold for 2 hours, then ramp to 1250°C at 10°C/min, hold for 30 mins, then quench; Cooling rate: >100°C/s (water quench).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a transient CaO layer on the surface of the hydride particles and the local suppression of oxygen activity in the gas phase, which kinetically inhibits the nucleation of alpha-HCP Ti/Zr-rich phases and stabilizes the high-temperature beta-BCC lattice.
generation.mechanism: The decomposition of CaH2 (CaH2 -> Ca + H2) and subsequent oxidation (Ca + O2 -> CaO) consumes dissolved oxygen and lowers the oxygen partial pressure below the critical threshold required for alpha-phase stabilization. The rapid quenching suppresses the diffusion-controlled transformation from beta-BCC to alpha-BCC + beta-BCC, trapping the single-phase beta-BCC structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: A nearly fully dense (>98% theoretical density) equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy exhibiting a single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) beta-structure with a grain size of 10-20 micrometers, with no detectable alpha-HCP phases or alpha-Ti precipitates.
generation.baseline: Standard sintering of HfNbTaTiZr hydride blends without a reactive getter or with a passive getter (e.g., Ti powder) typically results in residual oxygen levels >200 ppm, leading to a dual-phase (alpha-BCC + beta-BCC) microstructure after slow cooling and the formation of brittle alpha-Ti precipitates even after quenching due to insufficient oxygen removal.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis holds only if the CaH2 decomposition temperature (approx. 800-900°C) overlaps sufficiently with the TaH0.5 decomposition window; if the getter decomposes too early or too late, oxygen scavenging will be ineffective during the critical alloying phase.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the exact kinetics of oxygen diffusion through the forming oxide layer on the CaH2 particles versus the rate of hydride decomposition; if the oxide layer passivates the CaH2 too quickly, the oxygen scavenging may be incomplete, leading to trace alpha-phase formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction (XRD) on a thin-film sample of the HfNbTaTiZr-CaH2 blend inside a high-temperature furnace with controlled oxygen partial pressure. Ramp the temperature from 300°C to 1300°C at 5°C/min while continuously monitoring diffraction patterns, then immediately quench the sample in situ (or rapidly transfer to a cold stage) and monitor the cooling phase.
measurements: Lattice parameter shifts of the BCC phase indicating oxygen dissolution
Intensity evolution of alpha-HCP (Ti/Zr) peaks during the 800-1000°C window
Intensity evolution of alpha-Ti specific peaks
Disappearance of hydride peaks (TaH0.5, NbH, etc.)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if distinct alpha-HCP or alpha-Ti diffraction peaks appear with intensity >0.5% of the total diffraction intensity during the temperature window of 800-1000°C (the critical decomposition and getter activation window), or if the single-phase beta-BCC structure is not retained after the rapid quench (i.e., if alpha-phase peaks appear post-quench).

cited_evidence.text: Abstract A NbMoTaWVTi refractory high entropy alloy (HEA) has been successfully synthesized by mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS). The microstructure and mechanical properties of this alloy are investigated. It is observed that only two types of body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solutions are formed in the powders after ball milling for 40 h. However, a new face-centered cubic (FCC) precipitated phase is observed in the BCC matrix of bulk material consolidated by SPS. The FCC precipitated phase is identified as TiO, due to the introduction of O during the preparing process of HEA. The compressive yield strength, fracture strength, and total fracture strain of the consolidated bulk HEA are 2709 MPa, 3115 MPa, and 11.4%, respectively. The excellent mechanical properties can be attributed to solid solution strengthening and grain boundary strengthening of the fine-grained BCC matrix, as well as the precipitation strengthening owing to the formation of TiO particles. Keywords: refractory high entropy alloy, microstructure, mechanical properties

High entropy alloys (HEAs), complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), and multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) are the most common names of a new group of materials [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] ] introduced by Yeh et al. [ [6] ] and Cantor et al. [ [7] ] in the beginning of this century. Many definitions were proposed for such materials, but in general they consist of multiple (usually at least five) elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic composition [ [2] ]. This approach is different from the traditional alloy design using one (or maximum two) principal element and other minor elements. The presence of many elements in equiatomic (or near) composition leads to high mixing entropy and thus to many interesting properties [ [2] , [5] ]. One of such effects is the existence of a random solid solution and simple body centered cubic (bcc) or faced centered cubic (fcc) structure. Recently HEAs with hexagonal closed packed (hcp) structure have been reported as well [ [8] , [9] ]. A new approach to HEA design using the valence electron concentration (VEC) was recently proposed with the aim of increasing the plasticity of these alloys [ [10] , [11] ]. High entropy or multi principal element alloys are a promising and relatively young concept for designing alloys. The idea of creating alloys without a single main alloying element opens up a wide space for possible new alloy compositions. High entropy alloys based on refractory metals such as W, Mo, Ta or Nb are of interest for future high temperature applications e.g., in the aerospace or chemical industry. However, producing refractory metal high entropy alloys by conventional metallurgical methods remains challenging. For this reason, the feasibility of laser-based additive manufacturing of the refractory metal high entropy alloy W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 by laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) is investigated in the present work. In-situ alloy formation from mixtures of easily available elemental powders is employed to avoid an expensive atomization of pre-alloyed powder. It is shown that PBF-LB/M of W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 is in general possible and that a complete fusion of the powder mixture without a significant number of undissolved particles is achievable by in-situ alloy formation during PBF-LB/M when selecting favorable process parameter combinations.
